AMIP and additive one-step Newton are heuristics with possible false negatives. Refitting rules out false positives but cannot certify that no smaller harmful subset exists. Consequently, claims that MT-Bench “requires” more than 3% or 4% deletion, and the paper's classification of unsuccessful searches as robustness, are unsupported. There is no exhaustive small-instance comparison, approximation-recall study, lower bound, or robustness certificate.

The formal top-k definition is defective: K_T(w) is defined as a set of numerical score values rather than model identities, so comparing K_T(1) and K_T(w) generally detects ordinary score changes rather than membership changes. The evaluation lacks essential baselines and ablations: random deletion, a simple direct-head-to-head deletion heuristic, brute-force search on tractable cases, AMIP versus one-step Newton accuracy, and alternative ranking specifications. Most importantly, ties are discarded even though the deployed Chatbot Arena ranking incorporates them, so the headline results do not directly audit the system named in the claims.

Reporting deletion size as a fraction of the entire arena exaggerates the practical interpretation. For example, all nine top-1 deletions are direct wins between the affected models and may constitute a substantial fraction of the relevant head-to-head evidence. Total model appearance counts do not address this. Confidence intervals, bootstrap rank uncertainty, and random-perturbation comparisons are absent, although the affected models have extremely close scores and such flips may simply reflect unresolved statistical ties.

The conclusions comparing MT-Bench with Chatbot Arena and human with LLM judges are confounded by different model pools, score gaps, comparison graphs, dataset sizes, prompt distributions, and tie rates. No matched experiment or uncertainty analysis supports attributing the difference to expert annotators or prompt quality. The response-similarity claim is likewise based on only five manually selected examples without a quantitative or blinded assessment.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the purported code URL is blank, and preprocessing, model inclusion, solver details, and the search over deletion budgets are underspecified. Results are also internally inconsistent: page 13 reports 20 deletions for the human top-5 flip, whereas Figure 3 and Appendix B report five, while raw and tie-filtered denominators are mixed.

The methodological novelty is limited to applying an existing influence-based deletion heuristic to Bradley-Terry logistic regression; the pairwise top-k proposition is elementary. Given the technical errors and missing validation, this incremental contribution is not yet competitive for a top-tier AI conference.
